title: Random Spiking Neural Networks are Stable and Spectrally Simple
claim: Empirical noise sensitivity stays well below the theoretical bound and decreases as input dimension grows, across neuron types and time steps.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots with shared style, legend at right of each, (a)/(b) labels below, dashed bound line on top
description: Two side-by-side line charts with matching axes. Panel (a) shows sIF neurons and panel (b) shows IF neurons. Each plots expected noise sensitivity (ENS at ν=1/√n) on the y-axis against the number of features n (2, 3, 4) on the x-axis. Ten colored lines with circular markers, one for each time step t=0 to t=9, sit tightly clustered near 0.05–0.15 and slope slightly downward. A dark dashed 'Bound' curve sits far above them, starting around 0.73 and falling to about 0.46. A legend lists the time steps and the bound at the right of each plot. The eye goes first to the large gap between the dashed bound and the clustered colored curves. The panels are labeled (a) and (b) below.
caption: Noise sensitivity $\operatorname{ENS}_{1/\sqrt{n}}$ for different input dimensions $n$ for sIF and IF neurons with $\theta = 0.5$ and $T=10$. (a) sIF neuron (log-scale x-axis); dashed line: scaled bound from Theorem [ref]. (b) IF neuron (log-scale x-axis); dashed line: scaled bound from Theorem [ref].
abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are a promising paradigm for energy-efficient computation, yet their theoretical foundations-especially regarding stability and robustness-remain limited compared to artificial neural networks. In this work, we study discrete-time leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) SNNs through the lens of Boolean function analysis. We focus on noise sensitivity and stability in classification tasks, quantifying how input perturbations affect outputs. Our main result shows that wide LIF-SNN classifiers are stable on average, a property explained by the concentration of their Fourier spectrum on low-frequency components. Motivated by this, we introduce the notion of spectral simplicity, which formalizes simplicity in terms of Fourier spectrum concentration and connects our analysis to the simplicity bias observed in deep networks. Within this framework, we show that random LIF-SNNs are biased toward simple functions. Experiments on trained networks confirm that these stability properties persist in practice. Together, these results provide new insights into the stability and robustness properties of SNNs.
